[[File:Quadrat sample.JPG|thumb|A quadrat used to measure the percentage cover of certain species]]
A '''quadrat''' is a frame used in [[ecology]], [[geography]], and [[biology]] to isolate a standard unit of area for study of the distribution of an item over a large area. Quadrats typically occupy an area of 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> and are traditionally square, but modern quadrats can be rectangular, circular, or irregular.<ref>{{cite book |last=Krebs |first=C.J. |title=Ecological Methodology |year=1999 |publisher=Addison-Wesley }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Wheater |first=C. Philip |title=Practical Field Ecology: Project Guide |year=2011 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |display-authors=etal }}</ref> A quadrat is suitable for sampling or observing [[plants]], slow-moving animals, and some aquatic organisms.

A photo-quadrat is a photographic record of the area framed by a quadrat. It may use a physical frame to indicate the area, or may rely on fixed camera distance and lens [[field of view]] to automatically cover the specified area of substrate.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Littler |first1=M. M. |title=Handbook of Phycological Methods |last2=Littler |first2=D. S. |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=1985 |isbn=9780521249157 |volume=4. Ecological Field Methods: Macroalgae. |location=[[Cambridge, UK]] |pages=161–175 |chapter=Nondestructive sampling}}</ref> Parallel laser pointers mounted on the camera can also be used as scale indicators. The photo is taken perpendicular to the surface, or as close as possible to perpendicular for uneven surfaces.

==History==

The systematic use of quadrats was developed by the pioneering plant ecologists Roscoe Pound and [[Frederic Clements]] between 1898<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Pound, R. |author2=Clements, F. E. |author2-link=F. E. Clements |title=A method of determining the abundance of secondary species |journal=Minnesota Botanical Studies |volume=2 |pages=19–24 |date=June 1898}}</ref> and 1900.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Pound, R. |author2=Clements, F. E. |author2-link=F. E. Clements |title=Phytogeography of Nebraska |edition=Second |pages=[https://archive.org/details/phytogeographyn00poungoog/page/n69 61]–63 |date=1900 |url=https://archive.org/details/phytogeographyn00poungoog|publisher=Lincoln, Neb. Published by the Seminar }}</ref> The method was then swiftly applied for many purposes in [[ecology]], such as the study of [[ecological succession|plant succession]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Clements, F. E. |author-link=F. E. Clements |title=Plant Succession |publisher=The Seminar, Lincoln, Nebraska |pages=423–437 |date=1916}}</ref> Botanists and ecologists such as [[Arthur Tansley]] soon took up and modified the method.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Oliver, F. W. |author2=Tansley, A. G. |author2-link=Arthur Tansley |title=Methods of surveying vegetation on a large scale |journal=New Phytologist |volume=3 |pages=228–237 |date=December 1904 |issue=9–10 |url=https://archive.org/details/newphytologist3190tans |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1904.tb05867.x|doi-access=free |bibcode=1904NewPh...3..228O }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Tansley, A. G. |author-link=Arthur Tansley |title=Types of British vegetation |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=1911 |url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924001717820}}</ref>

The ecologist [[John Ernst Weaver]] applied the use of quadrats to the teaching of ecology in 1918.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weaver |first1=J. E. |title=The Quadrat Method in Teaching Ecology |journal=The Plant World |date=November 1919 |volume=21 |issue=11 |pages=267–283 |jstor=43477708}}</ref>

==Method==

A quadrat can be used by researchers to methodically count organisms within a smaller, representative area in order to extrapolate to a larger [[habitat]] when comprehensive sampling is impossible or not practical. The quadrat's size corresponds to the size of the organism being sampled and the overall sampling area. To avoid [[selection bias]], researchers randomly distribute quadrats throughout the sampling area.<ref name="SPS">{{cite web |title=Questions about Quadrats |url=http://www.saps.org.uk/secondary/teaching-resources/260-questions-about-quadrats |access-date=20 June 2018 |publisher=Science and Plants for Schools}}</ref>

[[File:Botanist and students examining the species distribution using quadrat.jpg|thumb|Botanist and students examining the species distribution using a quadrat|214x214px]]For long-term studies, the same quadrats can be revisited after their initial sampling. Methods of precisely relocating the area of study vary widely in accuracy and include measurement from nearby permanent markers, use of [[total station]] [[Theodolite|theodolites]], consumer-grade [[GPS]], and [[differential GPS]].<ref name="Dodd">{{cite journal | last1=Dodd | first1=M. | title=Where are my quadrats? Positional accuracy in fieldwork | journal =Methods in Ecology and Evolution | volume=2 | issue=6 | pages=576–584 | year=2011 | doi=10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00118.x | doi-access=free | bibcode=2011MEcEv...2..576D }}</ref>
